mistakes: Searching every row: O(rows · log cols) is fine, but O(log(rows · cols)) is possible.
Mixing up row = mid // cols and col = mid % cols.
exercises.followup: Rows and columns are sorted separately (not overall): start from the top-right corner.

exercises.title: Koko Eating Bananas
exercises.prompt:
Piles of bananas; each hour Koko eats up to k bananas from one pile. Return the minimum integer k so she finishes all piles within h hours.

`([3, 6, 7, 11], 8)` → `4`
hints: If speed k is enough, any faster speed is too.
Binary search k between 1 and max(piles); check a speed in O(n).
Approach: Binary search on the answer with an O(n) feasibility check.
mistakes: Using hours += pile // k, which drops the partial hour.
Searching speeds up to sum(piles) instead of max(piles).
exercises.followup: Each pile also has an earliest start time.

exercises.title: Capacity to Ship Within D Days
exercises.prompt: Packages must ship in order; each day the ship carries a contiguous group with total weight ≤ capacity. Return the least capacity that ships everything within `days` days.
hints: The capacity is at least max(weights) and at most sum(weights).
For a given capacity, a greedy pass counts the days needed.
Approach: Binary search on capacity + greedy check.
mistakes: Starting the search below max(weights) (one package must fit).
Counting days incorrectly when a package starts a new day.
exercises.followup: Return the split of packages per day, too.

exercises.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
exercises.prompt: Return the median of two sorted lists, in O(log(min(n, m))).
hints: Merging is O(n + m). For O(log), binary search how many elements the left half takes from the shorter list.
A split is right when every left-side value ≤ every right-side value.
Approach: Binary search the partition of the shorter array.
mistakes: Merging both lists (O(n + m)), which misses the goal.
Binary searching the longer list, which causes index errors.
exercises.followup: Find the k-th smallest of the two lists.

exercises.title: Split Array Largest Sum
exercises.prompt:
Split the list into k non-empty contiguous parts so that the largest part-sum is as small as possible. Return that sum.

`([7, 2, 5, 10, 8], 2)` → `18`
hints: Guess the answer L. Can you split into ≤ k parts with every sum ≤ L? A greedy pass tells you.
If L works, any bigger L works: binary search.
Approach: Binary search on the answer + greedy feasibility (same shape as shipping capacity).
mistakes: A greedy check that starts a new part one element too late.
A low bound of 0 instead of max(nums).
exercises.followup: Return the parts as well.

exercises.title: The last element is never checked
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.

exercises.title: Binary search on unsorted data
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bs-d4` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.

exercises.title: Not the FIRST occurrence

exercises.title: Bubble Sort
exercises.prompt: Sort the list in place with bubble sort and return it. Stop early if a pass makes no swaps.
hints: Compare neighbours; swap when out of order.
After pass i, the last i items are in place.
Approach: Repeated neighbour swaps with an early exit.
mistakes: Comparing a[i] with a[i + 1] up to the very end, causing IndexError.
Not stopping early when a pass makes no swaps.
exercises.followup: Count the number of swaps (it equals the number of inversions).

exercises.title: Selection Sort
exercises.prompt: Sort in place with selection sort and return the list.
hints: Find the minimum of a[i:], swap it into position i.
For each position i, find the smallest element in a[i:] and swap it into position i.
Approach: Select the minimum each pass.
mistakes: Swapping on every smaller element instead of once per pass.
Searching for the minimum from index 0 every time.
exercises.followup: Is selection sort stable? Find an example.

exercises.title: Insertion Sort
exercises.prompt: Sort in place with insertion sort and return the list.
hints: Keep the left part sorted. Take the next item and shift bigger ones right until its place opens up.
Take a[i], shift larger elements of the sorted prefix one place right, then drop a[i] into the gap.
Approach: Grow a sorted prefix.
mistakes: Swapping repeatedly instead of shifting and inserting once.
Moving equal elements past each other (breaks stability).
exercises.followup: Use binary search to find the insertion point.

exercises.title: Counting Sort
exercises.prompt: All values are integers in 0..k. Return them sorted without comparisons.
hints: Count how many of each value there are.
Count each value in a list of size k + 1, then write each value count times.
Approach: Count per value, then write values out in order.
mistakes: Allocating counts of size max(nums) when k is given (or vice versa).
Comparing elements (that is not counting sort).
exercises.followup: Make it stable for sorting records by a small integer key.

exercises.title: Sort People
exercises.prompt: Sort (name, age) pairs by age ascending; equal ages by name alphabetically.
hints: A tuple key sorts by the first item, then the second.
Use sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0])).
Approach: sorted with a tuple key.
mistakes: Sorting twice in the wrong order (sort by name first, then by age, relies on stability).
Sorting by name descending.
exercises.followup: Sort by age descending but names ascending.

exercises.title: Can Attend All Meetings
exercises.prompt: Given meeting intervals [start, end], return True if no two overlap (a meeting ending at t and one starting at t do not overlap).
hints: After sorting by start time, only neighbours can overlap.
Sort by start time, then compare each meeting with the one before it.
Approach: Sort by start; compare each start with the previous end.
mistakes: Not sorting first.
Using >= when comparing, which flags back-to-back meetings.
exercises.followup: Return the minimum number of rooms (hp-meeting-rooms).

exercises.title: Minimum Absolute Difference Pairs
exercises.prompt: Return all pairs [a, b] (a < b) of distinct integers with the minimum absolute difference, in ascending order.
hints: After sorting, the closest pairs are neighbours.
After sorting, the closest pairs are neighbours.
Approach: Sort, then scan adjacent differences.
mistakes: Comparing every pair: O(n²).
Forgetting to sort first.
exercises.followup: Return just the minimum difference for a stream of insertions.

exercises.title: Relative Sort Array
exercises.prompt: Sort `arr1` so that values appear in the order given by `arr2`; values not in arr2 go at the end in ascending order.
hints: Give every value in arr2 a rank; everything else gets a rank after all of them.
Map each value of arr2 to its position, then sort with key (position or len(arr2), value).
Approach: Custom sort key (rank, value).
constraints: values of arr2 are distinct and all appear in arr1
mistakes: Sorting the leftover values in arr1 order instead of ascending.
Using arr2.index() inside the key: O(n · m).
exercises.followup: Do it with counting sort when values are small.

exercises.title: Merge Sort
exercises.prompt: Return a new sorted list using merge sort (no sorted()/sort()).
hints: Base case: 0 or 1 items are sorted.
Sort each half recursively, then merge with two pointers.
Approach: Divide and conquer.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
mistakes: Merging with list.pop(0), which is O(n) per pop.
Forgetting to copy what is left of one half.
exercises.followup: Make it stable and prove that it is.

exercises.title: Quick Sort
exercises.prompt: Sort the list in place with quick sort (Lomuto or Hoare partition) and return it.
hints: Partition: move everything smaller than the pivot to the left, then put the pivot right after them.
Recurse on the two sides. Pick a random pivot to stay fast on sorted input.
Approach: Partition around a random pivot, recurse.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) expected, O(n²) worst
mistakes: Always picking the first element as pivot: O(n²) on sorted input.
Partition loops that never end when all values are equal.
exercises.followup: Use a random pivot and a three-way partition for many duplicates.

tests.label: 3,000 already-sorted items (a fixed last-element pivot recurses too deep)

exercises.title: Kth Largest Element
exercises.prompt: Return the k-th largest element (k = 1 is the maximum). Try to beat O(n log n): quickselect averages O(n).
hints: Sorting works in O(n log n). A min-heap of size k gives O(n log k).
Quickselect: partition like quick sort, but recurse into only the side that contains the target index.
Approach: Quickselect (or heap of size k).
mistakes: Sorting ascending and returning nums[k].
A quickselect without random pivots, which is slow on sorted input.
exercises.followup: Solve it with a min-heap of size k and compare.

exercises.title: Largest Number
exercises.prompt:
Arrange the non-negative integers to form the largest number; return it as a string.

`[3, 30, 34, 5, 9]` → `"9534330"`
hints: Which should come first, "3" or "30"? Compare "330" with "303".
Sort with a comparator: a before b if a + b > b + a. functools.cmp_to_key turns a comparator into a key.
Approach: Custom comparator sort.
mistakes: Sorting numerically or as plain strings.
Returning "00" for [0, 0].
exercises.followup: Same comparator idea: the smallest number instead.

exercises.title: H-Index
exercises.prompt: The h-index is the largest h such that the researcher has at least h papers with ≥ h citations each.
hints: Sort descending: the i-th paper (1-based) has c[i − 1] citations.
h grows while the h-th paper still has at least h citations.
Approach: Sort descending and scan.
mistakes: Off-by-one between "at least h papers" and indexes.
Sorting ascending and counting from the wrong end.
exercises.followup: Do it in O(n) with counting.

exercises.title: Count Inversions
exercises.prompt: Count pairs i < j with nums[i] > nums[j], in O(n log n).
hints: Checking every pair is O(n²).
During merge sort, when you take from the right half, every element still waiting in the left half forms an inversion with it.
Approach: Merge sort that counts while merging.
mistakes: Adding 1 instead of the number of remaining left elements when a right element is smaller.
Two nested loops: O(n²).
exercises.followup: Count inversions with a Fenwick tree (rq-count-smaller).

exercises.title: Maximum Gap
exercises.prompt: Return the largest difference between two neighbours in the sorted order of the list, or 0 for fewer than two numbers. Try to do it in O(n) time with buckets instead of sorting.
hints: Sorting gives O(n log n). For O(n): with n numbers between lo and hi, the biggest gap is at least (hi − lo) / (n − 1).
Make buckets of that width. The biggest gap can never be inside one bucket, so keep only each bucket’s min and max and compare neighbouring non-empty buckets.
Approach: Pigeonhole bucketing: track min and max per bucket and scan the buckets.
mistakes: Comparing neighbours in the original (unsorted) order.
A bucket width of 0 when all numbers are close (use max(1, …)).
Looking for the gap inside a bucket instead of between buckets.
exercises.followup: Solve it with radix sort and compare the two O(n) approaches.

exercises.title: Index out of range
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test so-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.

exercises.title: k-th largest, off by one

exercises.title: Merge sort loses numbers
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.

exercises.title: Preorder Traversal
exercises.prompt: Return the preorder traversal (root, left, right) as a list.
hints: Handle None, then combine: node, left result, right result.
Visit the node, then recurse on left, then right.
Approach: Recursive DFS (or an explicit stack).
mistakes: Appending the root after the children (that is postorder).
Forgetting the None base case.
exercises.followup: Write it iteratively with a stack.

exercises.title: Inorder Traversal
exercises.prompt: Return the inorder traversal (left, root, right). Bonus: do it without recursion, using a stack.
hints: Recursive version: left list + [val] + right list.
Iterative: push nodes while going left; pop one, visit it, then go to its right child.
Approach: Recursion, or a stack simulating it.
mistakes: Pushing right children before going left in the iterative version.
Forgetting the None base case.
exercises.followup: Morris traversal: O(1) extra space.

exercises.title: Postorder Traversal
exercises.prompt: Return the postorder traversal (left, right, root).
hints: Same shape as preorder, with the node last.
Recurse left, recurse right, then append the node’s value.
Approach: Recursive DFS.
mistakes: Visiting the root before its children.
In the iterative version, reversing the wrong traversal.
exercises.followup: Iterative postorder with one stack.

exercises.title: Maximum Depth
exercises.prompt: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
hints: An empty tree has depth 0.
Recursion: handle the empty tree (None) first, then combine the answers of the left and right subtrees.
Approach: 1 + the deeper subtree.
mistakes: Returning 1 for an empty tree.
Counting edges instead of nodes.
exercises.followup: Solve it iteratively with BFS, counting levels.

exercises.title: Minimum Depth
exercises.prompt: Return the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root to a leaf.
hints: Careful: a node with one child is not a leaf, so min(left, right) of a missing side is wrong.
BFS can stop at the first leaf it sees.
Approach: BFS to the first leaf.
mistakes: Taking min(left, right) when one side is empty (a node with one child is not a leaf).
exercises.followup: Solve it with BFS, stopping at the first leaf.

exercises.title: Count Nodes
exercises.prompt: Return the number of nodes in the tree.
hints: 1 for this node plus the counts of both subtrees.
Recursion: handle the empty tree (None) first, then combine the answers of the left and right subtrees.
Approach: Tree recursion.
mistakes: Forgetting to count the node itself.
Returning 1 for an empty tree.
exercises.followup: Count the nodes of a complete binary tree in O(log² n).

exercises.title: Sum of Leaves
exercises.prompt: Return the sum of the values of all leaves.
hints: Two base cases: None (0) and a leaf (its value).
A leaf has no left and no right child; return its value, otherwise sum the two subtrees.
Approach: Recursion with a leaf check.
mistakes: Counting nodes with one child as leaves.
Adding internal node values.
exercises.followup: Sum only the left leaves.

exercises.title: Invert Binary Tree
exercises.prompt: Mirror the tree (swap every left and right child) and return its root.
hints: Invert each subtree, then swap them.
Swap the children of each node, then invert both subtrees.
Approach: Recursive swap.
mistakes: Swapping only the root’s children.
Overwriting one child before saving it.
exercises.followup: Do it iteratively with a queue.

exercises.title: Same Tree
exercises.prompt: Return True if two trees have the same shape and values.
hints: Both None → True; exactly one None → False.
Two empty trees are the same; one empty is not; otherwise compare values and both subtrees.
Approach: Compare roots, then both pairs of subtrees.
mistakes: Comparing only values, not shape.
Not handling the case where exactly one node is None.
exercises.followup: Check whether two trees are mirror images.

exercises.title: Symmetric Tree
exercises.prompt: Return True if the tree is a mirror of itself.
hints: Compare two trees that should be mirror images: left with right, outer with outer, inner with inner.
Write a helper mirror(a, b): values equal, a.left mirrors b.right and a.right mirrors b.left.
Approach: Mirror comparison helper.
mistakes: Comparing left with left instead of left with right.
Checking only that each level is a palindrome (shape matters).
exercises.followup: Solve it iteratively with a queue of node pairs.

exercises.title: Path Sum
exercises.prompt: Return True if some root-to-leaf path adds up to target.
hints: Subtract the node’s value and pass the remainder down.
Only check the remainder at a leaf.
Approach: DFS carrying the remaining sum.
mistakes: Checking the sum at internal nodes instead of leaves.
Returning True for an empty tree and target 0.
exercises.followup: Return all root-to-leaf paths with the target sum.

exercises.title: Average of Levels
exercises.prompt: Return the average value of each level, top to bottom.
hints: Level-order BFS, summing each level.
BFS level by level: sum the values of a level and divide by its size.
Approach: BFS by levels.
mistakes: Using integer division.
Averaging over the whole tree.
exercises.followup: Return the maximum of each level.

exercises.title: Level Order Traversal
exercises.prompt:
Return the values level by level, as a list of lists.

`[3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7]` → `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`
hints: BFS with a queue (deque is available).
Process exactly len(queue) nodes per round: that is one level.
Approach: BFS, one level per round.
mistakes: Mixing levels because you do not process the queue one level at a time.
Using a list with pop(0): O(n) per pop.
exercises.followup: Return the levels bottom-up.

exercises.title: All Root-to-Leaf Paths
exercises.prompt: Return every root-to-leaf path as a string like `"1->2->5"`, left to right.
hints: Carry the path so far down the recursion; record it at leaves.
Carry the path so far down the recursion; at a leaf, join it with "->".
Approach: DFS with the current path.
mistakes: Adding a path at a node with one child.
Building strings with a shared list that is not undone.
exercises.followup: Return the path with the largest sum.

exercises.title: Diameter of a Binary Tree
exercises.prompt: Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes (it need not pass through the root).
hints: The longest path bends at some node: left height + right height.
Compute heights bottom-up and update a best value as you go: one pass.
Approach: Postorder heights + a running maximum.
mistakes: Assuming the longest path passes through the root.
Counting nodes instead of edges.
exercises.followup: Return the diameter of an n-ary tree.

exercises.title: Balanced Binary Tree
exercises.prompt: A tree is height-balanced if, at every node, the subtree heights differ by at most 1. Check it in O(n).
hints: Calling height() at every node is O(n²).
Return the height and the verdict together; use −1 to mean “not balanced”.
Approach: One postorder pass returning height or −1.
mistakes: Calling height() at every node: O(n²).
Checking balance only at the root.
exercises.followup: Return the height difference that is largest anywhere in the tree.

exercises.title: Right Side View
exercises.prompt: Return the values you would see standing on the right of the tree, top to bottom.
hints: The visible node of each level is its rightmost node.
BFS by levels; take the last node of each level (or the first, if you enqueue right before left).
Approach: BFS by levels.
mistakes: Following only right children (left nodes can be visible).
Taking the first node of each level instead of the last.
exercises.followup: Return the left side view.

exercises.title: Zigzag Level Order
exercises.prompt: Level order, but alternate direction each level: left→right, then right→left, …
hints: Normal level order, then reverse every other level.
Do a normal level order, and reverse every second level before adding it.
Approach: BFS by levels + a direction flag.
mistakes: Reversing the order you visit children (that changes the next level).
Reversing every level.
exercises.followup: Use a deque and append on alternate sides instead of reversing.

exercises.title: Subtree of Another Tree
exercises.prompt: Return True if `sub` appears in `root` as a node together with all its descendants.
hints: At every node of root, ask: is the tree starting here the same as sub?
At every node of root, check is_same(node, sub).
Approach: Same-tree check at every node.
constraints: 1 ≤ nodes in root ≤ 2000, 1 ≤ nodes in sub ≤ 1000
mistakes: Matching values but not the full subtree below (extra descendants).
Only checking the root of root.
exercises.followup: Solve it in O(n + m) by serialising both trees and searching for a substring.

exercises.title: Lowest Common Ancestor
exercises.prompt: Values are distinct. Return the value of the lowest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant).
hints: Let each subtree report whether it contains p or q.
If p is found in the left subtree and q in the right, the current node is the answer.
Approach: Postorder: return the found node upward; the first node with hits on both sides is the LCA.
mistakes: Returning the deeper of p and q instead of their ancestor.
Searching each subtree twice (O(n²)).

exercises.title: Maximum Path Sum
exercises.prompt: A path is any sequence of connected nodes (it does not need to pass through the root). Return the maximum sum of a non-empty path.
hints: Like the diameter: the best path bends at some node, using its best left and right downward branches.
A branch with a negative sum is better left out: max(gain, 0).
Approach: Postorder gains + global best.
mistakes: Returning a path that branches (both children) to the parent.
Not ignoring negative child contributions (use max(0, gain)).
exercises.followup: Return the path’s nodes, not just its sum.

exercises.title: Build Tree From Preorder and Inorder
exercises.prompt: Values are distinct. Rebuild the tree from its preorder and inorder traversals.
hints: The first preorder value is the root. Find it in inorder: everything left of it is the left subtree.
A dict from value to inorder index makes each split O(1).
Approach: Recursive split using preorder roots and inorder positions.
mistakes: Using inorder.index() in every call: O(n²).
Mixing up the sizes of the left and right parts.
exercises.followup: Rebuild from inorder and postorder instead.

Write "#" for None; deserialize by reading values in the same preorder.

mistakes: Not marking missing children, so different shapes give the same string.
Splitting on commas when values may be negative or multi-digit without a separator.

exercises.title: Search in a BST
exercises.prompt: Return the node with value target (or None). Use the BST property: O(h).
hints: Compare with the current node and go left or right.
Go left if target is smaller than the node, right if larger.

Returning the value instead of the node.

exercises.followup: Find the second smallest value in O(h).

exercises.title: Range Sum of a BST
exercises.prompt: Return the sum of values in [low, high]. Skip subtrees that cannot contain such values.
hints: If root.val < low, nothing on its left can be in range.
If node  high, only the left.
Approach: DFS with pruning.
mistakes: Visiting subtrees that cannot contain values in range.
Using exclusive bounds.
exercises.followup: Count the nodes in the range instead.

exercises.title: Closest Value
exercises.prompt: Return the value in the BST closest to a float target (the smaller one on a tie).
hints: The closest value lies on the search path for target.
Walk down like a search, keeping the closest value seen so far.
Approach: Walk the search path, tracking the best.
mistakes: Exploring both subtrees.
Ignoring the tie rule (return the smaller value).
exercises.followup: Return the k closest values.

exercises.title: Validate a BST
exercises.prompt: Return True if the tree is a valid BST (strictly smaller left, strictly larger right, for all descendants).
hints: Checking only children is not enough.
Pass down the allowed range (low, high); or check that the inorder traversal is strictly increasing.
Approach: Range checking DFS.
mistakes: Only comparing a node with its direct children.
Using <= so equal values pass.
exercises.followup: Validate using an inorder traversal instead of bounds.

exercises.title: Kth Smallest in a BST
exercises.prompt: Return the k-th smallest value (1-based).
hints: Inorder visits values in ascending order.
Stop as soon as you have visited k nodes (iterative inorder makes stopping easy).
Approach: Inorder traversal, stop at the k-th visit.
mistakes: Collecting the whole inorder list when you can stop at k.
Off-by-one: k is 1-based.
exercises.followup: The tree changes often: store subtree sizes to answer in O(h).

exercises.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST
exercises.prompt: Return the value of the lowest common ancestor of values p and q, using the BST property (no need to search both subtrees).
hints: If both values are smaller than the node, the answer is in the left subtree.
The first node where they split (or that equals one of them) is the answer.
Approach: Walk down until p and q are on different sides.
mistakes: Searching both subtrees like in a general tree.
Not handling the case where p is an ancestor of q.
exercises.followup: Solve it iteratively in O(1) space.

exercises.title: Sorted List to Balanced BST
exercises.prompt: Build a height-balanced BST from a sorted list of distinct numbers.
hints: Which value should be the root so both sides have the same size?
The middle element, then recurse on each half.
Approach: Divide and conquer on the middle element.
mistakes: Inserting values one by one in order, which builds a linked list.
Slicing in every call (O(n log n) copying); pass indexes.
exercises.followup: Build it from a sorted linked list.

exercises.title: Delete Node in a BST
exercises.prompt: Delete the node with value key (if present) and return the root. The result must still be a valid BST.
hints: Find the node first, like a search.
Three cases: leaf, one child (return the child), two children (copy the successor, then delete it from the right subtree).
Approach: Recursive delete with the in-order successor.
mistakes: Losing the subtree of a node with one child.
For two children, forgetting to delete the successor from the right subtree.
exercises.followup: Delete all nodes in a value range.

tests.label: delete a node with two children

exercises.title: Two Sum in a BST
exercises.prompt: Return True if two different nodes sum to k.
hints: Inorder gives a sorted list.
Then it is pair-sum on a sorted array: two pointers (or a set while traversing).
Approach: Inorder + two pointers.
mistakes: Using the same node twice (k = 2 × value).
Ignoring the BST: a set during any traversal works, but two pointers on the inorder list uses the order.
exercises.followup: Solve it with two BST iterators (one forward, one backward) in O(h) space.

exercises.title: Inorder Successor
exercises.prompt: Return the smallest value strictly greater than x, or None, in O(h).
hints: Every time you go left, the current node is a candidate.
Walk down: when the node is larger than x, it is a candidate and you go left; otherwise go right.
Approach: Search path, remembering the last “went left” node.
mistakes: Only looking in the right subtree (the successor may be an ancestor).
exercises.followup: Find the predecessor too.

exercises.title: Build a Binary Search Tree
exercises.prompt:
Implement a BST of distinct numbers. Smaller values go left, larger values go right.

Requirements:
- `insert(x)` (ignore duplicates)
- `contains(x)` → bool
- `inorder()` → sorted list
- `minimum()`, `maximum()` → value or None
- `delete(x)` handles leaves, one child and two children
- `height()`: number of levels (empty = 0)
hints: Recursive insert returns the (possibly new) subtree root: node.left = insert(node.left, x).
Delete with two children: copy the smallest value of the right subtree into the node, then delete that value from the right subtree.
Approach: Each operation follows one root-to-leaf path, guided by comparisons.
exercises.cx: O(h) per operation: O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst case

tests.label: insert (with a duplicate), search, min, max, height
delete a leaf, a node with two children, a node with one child

exercises.title: Recover a BST
exercises.prompt: Exactly two nodes of a binary search tree were swapped by mistake. Fix the tree in place by swapping their values back, and return the root.
hints: An inorder traversal of a BST is sorted. What does it look like after two values are swapped?
There are one or two places where a value is bigger than the next one. The first wrong node is the left side of the first drop; the second is the right side of the last drop.
Approach: Inorder traversal, remember the nodes at the order violations, swap their values.
exercises.cx: O(n) time, O(h) space (Morris traversal makes it O(1))
mistakes: Handling only the case of two drops: adjacent swapped nodes give a single drop.
Swapping nodes instead of values (much harder, and not needed).
exercises.followup: Do it with O(1) extra space using Morris inorder traversal.

exercises.title: Contains Nearby Almost Duplicate
exercises.prompt: Return `True` if there are two different indexes i and j with `|i − j| ≤ k` and `|nums[i] − nums[j]| ≤ t`. In languages with a balanced BST you would use a sorted set; in Python, use buckets of width t + 1.
hints: Keep only the last k values. Among them, is there one within t of x? A sorted structure answers that in O(log k).
Bucket trick: with width t + 1, two values in the same bucket always differ by ≤ t, and a close value can only be in the same or a neighbouring bucket.
Approach: Sliding window of buckets keyed by x // (t + 1).
mistakes: Using int(x / width), which rounds negative numbers towards zero and merges buckets −1 and 0.
Forgetting to remove the value that leaves the window.
exercises.followup: Solve it with a sorted list and bisect in O(n log k), then compare.

exercises.title: The new node vanishes
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bst-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
The returned subtree is never attached: write root.left = insert(root.left, v)
When root.left is None, insert returns a new node… which nobody stores.

exercises.title: Searching the wrong way
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bst-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
Directions are swapped: smaller targets are in the LEFT subtree
contains(build_tree([4, 2, 7]), 2) returns False.

exercises.title: Only checking the children
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bst-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
It only compares each node with its direct children, so [5, 4, 6, None, None, 3, 7] passes although 3 sits in 5’s right subtree
Pass the allowed (low, high) range down the recursion.

exercises.title: Last Stone Weight
exercises.prompt: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones x ≤ y: if equal both vanish, otherwise a stone of weight y − x remains. Return the last weight, or 0.
hints: You need the two largest values again and again: a max-heap.
Push negated weights into a heap; pop two, push back the difference if it is non-zero.
Approach: Max-heap via negation.
mistakes: Forgetting that heapq is a min-heap (negate the weights).
Re-sorting the list every round: works, but O(n² log n).
exercises.followup: Minimise the final weight (that becomes a partition DP).

exercises.title: Minimum Cost to Connect Ropes
exercises.prompt: Joining two ropes of lengths a and b costs a + b and makes one rope of length a + b. Return the minimum total cost to join all ropes.
hints: Long ropes that get joined early are paid for again and again.
Greedy: always join the two shortest.
Approach: Greedy with a min-heap (Huffman-style).
mistakes: Joining the ropes in the given order.
Forgetting that a single rope costs 0.
exercises.followup: Prove why joining the two shortest first is optimal.

exercises.title: Kth Largest Element (heap)
exercises.prompt: Return the k-th largest element using a heap of size k: O(n log k).
hints: Keep only the k largest values seen so far.
A min-heap makes the smallest of those k easy to evict.
Approach: Min-heap of size k.
mistakes: Using a max-heap of all n elements (O(n log n)).
Popping when the heap has k elements instead of more than k.
exercises.followup: Keep it working for a stream of numbers.

exercises.title: K Closest Points to the Origin
exercises.prompt: Return the k points closest to (0, 0), sorted by distance (ties: by x, then y).
hints: Compare squared distances (no square root needed).
A max-heap of size k, or heapq.nsmallest with a key.
Approach: Heap selection by squared distance.
mistakes: Using sqrt (unnecessary and slower).
Ignoring the tie-break rule.
exercises.followup: Solve it with quickselect in average O(n).

exercises.title: Sort a Nearly Sorted List
exercises.prompt: Each element is at most k positions away from its sorted position. Sort in O(n log k).
hints: The smallest remaining element must be among the next k + 1 elements.
Keep a min-heap of the next k + 1 elements; the smallest of them is the next in sorted order.
Approach: Sliding heap of size k + 1.
mistakes: Sorting the whole list (O(n log n)).
A heap of size k instead of k + 1.
exercises.followup: What if k is unknown?

exercises.title: Top K Frequent Words
exercises.prompt: Return the k most frequent words, most frequent first; ties alphabetically.
hints: Count first.
Order by (−count, word).
Approach: Counter + heap selection with a tuple key.
mistakes: Breaking ties in reverse alphabetical order in a heap.
Sorting by count only.
exercises.followup: Do it in O(n log k).

exercises.title: Meeting Rooms II
exercises.prompt: Return the minimum number of rooms needed for all meetings [start, end) (a meeting may start when another ends).
hints: Process meetings by start time.
Keep the end times of busy rooms in a min-heap: the earliest-ending room is the one to reuse.
Approach: Sort by start + min-heap of end times.
mistakes: Sorting by end time.
Not freeing a room when a meeting ends exactly when another starts.
exercises.followup: Return which room each meeting uses.

exercises.title: Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix
exercises.prompt: Each row and column is sorted ascending. Return the k-th smallest value.
hints: Treat each row as a sorted list and merge them with a heap.
Pop k − 1 times; the top is then the answer.
Approach: k-way merge with a heap.
mistakes: Flattening and sorting (O(n² log n)).
Pushing every element into the heap at once.
exercises.followup: Solve it with binary search on the value range.

exercises.title: Reorganize String
exercises.prompt: Rearrange the letters so no two adjacent letters are equal. Return any valid arrangement, or "" if impossible.
hints: Always place the most frequent letter that is not equal to the previous one.
A max-heap of (count, letter); hold back the letter you just used for one round.
Approach: Greedy with a max-heap and a one-step cooldown.
mistakes: Not checking impossibility: the most common letter can appear at most (n + 1) // 2 times.
Placing the most common letter repeatedly without alternating.
exercises.followup: Every two equal letters must be at least k apart.

exercises.title: Build a Min-Heap
exercises.prompt:
Implement a binary min-heap stored in a list: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, its parent at (i − 1) // 2. Do not use heapq.

Requirements:
- `push(x)`: append, then bubble up
- `pop()`: remove and return the minimum (move the last item to the root, then bubble down); raise `IndexError` if empty
- `peek()` → minimum; `IndexError` if empty
- `len(h)`
- push and pop in O(log n)
hints: Bubble up: while the item is smaller than its parent, swap with the parent.
Bubble down: swap with the SMALLER child while that child is smaller than the item.
Approach: Complete binary tree in a list; each fix walks one root-to-leaf path.

tests.label: push six numbers, pop them in order

exercises.title: Merge K Sorted Linked Lists
exercises.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists (`ListNode`, `build`, `to_list` are provided) into one sorted list.
hints: The next output node is the smallest among the k current fronts.
Keep the fronts in a heap; after popping a node, push its successor.
Approach: Heap of list fronts.
mistakes: Pushing ListNode objects directly (they cannot be compared); push (val, index, node).
Merging lists one by one: O(k · N).
exercises.followup: Merge k sorted Python lists lazily with a generator (heapq.merge).

exercises.title: Find Median From a Data Stream
exercises.prompt: Class `MedianFinder` with `add(num)` and `median()` (a float). Both must be fast for many operations.
hints: Sorting after every add is O(n log n) each.
Two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, kept the same size (± 1).
Approach: Two balanced heaps; the median sits at their tops.
mistakes: Sorting after every add: O(n log n) per add.
Letting the two heaps differ in size by more than one.
exercises.followup: Support removing numbers too (sliding-window median).

tests.call: (lambda m: [m.add(x) or m.median() for x in (5, 15, 1, 3)])(MedianFinder())

exercises.title: The “largest” is the smallest
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test hp-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
heapq is a MIN-heap: this returns the smallest value
Negate the values, use max(), or heapq.nlargest(1, nums)[0].

exercises.title: Sift down ignores a child
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test hp-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
It only ever looks at the LEFT child; it must swap with the smaller of the two children
sift_down([9, 4, 1], 0) gives [4, 9, 1], and 4 > 1 breaks the heap.

exercises.title: Equal priorities crash
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test hp-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
When two priorities are equal, Python compares the dicts next, and dicts cannot be ordered: TypeError
Add a unique tie-breaker: (priority, counter, job).

exercises.title: Longest Common Prefix
exercises.prompt: Return the longest prefix shared by all words ("" if none). (A trie works; so does comparing characters column by column.)
hints: In a trie, the common prefix is the path from the root while each node has exactly one child and is not a word end.
Simpler: zip(*words) gives columns of characters.
Approach: Column scan (or a single-branch walk in a trie).
mistakes: Crashing on an empty list or an empty word.
Comparing only the first two words.
exercises.followup: Find the longest prefix shared by at least half of the words.

exercises.title: Count Words With a Prefix
exercises.prompt: Build a trie from `words`, then return how many words start with each prefix in `queries`.
hints: Store at every node how many words pass through it.
Increase a counter in every node you pass while inserting; a query walks the prefix and reads its counter.
Approach: Trie with pass-through counts.
mistakes: Walking the whole subtree to count (store counts in nodes).
Counting a word once per matching letter.
exercises.followup: Support deleting words.

exercises.title: Replace Words
exercises.prompt:
Replace every word in the sentence by its shortest root from `roots` (if any root is a prefix of it).

`(["cat", "bat", "rat"], "the cattle was rattled by the battery")` → `"the cat was rat by the bat"`
hints: Put the roots in a trie.
Walk each word down the trie and stop at the first node that ends a root.
Insert all roots into a trie; for each word, walk until you hit an end-of-root marker.
Approach: Trie of roots; shortest match per word.
mistakes: Replacing with the longest root instead of the shortest.
Checking every root against every word: O(R · W).
exercises.followup: Roots can contain wildcards.

tests.call: replace_words(["cat", "bat", "rat"], "the cattle was rattled by the battery")

exercises.title: Search Suggestions
exercises.prompt: After each character typed of `search_word`, return up to 3 products (alphabetically smallest) starting with the typed prefix.
hints: Sort the products first so the first 3 you store at each node are the smallest.
Each node keeps up to 3 suggestions for its prefix.
Approach: Trie with up to 3 cached suggestions per node.
mistakes: Returning more than three products.
Not sorting the products first.
exercises.followup: Rank suggestions by popularity (projects/08_autocomplete).

exercises.title: Word Dictionary With Wildcards
exercises.prompt: Class `WordDictionary`: `add_word(w)`, and `search(w)` where `.` matches any one letter.
hints: Normal letters follow one child.
A dot must try every child: DFS.
Approach: Trie + DFS branching on wildcards.
exercises.cx: O(L) without dots; worse with many dots
constraints: words up to 25 letters, at most 2 dots per search
mistakes: Treating "." as a literal character.
Matching prefixes instead of whole words.
exercises.followup: Support "*" for any sequence of letters.

tests.call: (lambda d: (d.add_word("bad"), d.add_word("dad"), d.search("pad"), d.search(".ad"), d.search("b.."), d.search("..."), d.search("b"), d.search("....")))(WordDictionary())[2:]

exercises.title: Longest Word Built Letter by Letter
exercises.prompt:
Return the longest word that can be built one letter at a time, where every prefix is also in the list. Ties: the alphabetically smallest.

`["w", "wo", "wor", "worl", "world"]` → `"world"`
hints: Every prefix must itself be a word.
A trie where you only walk through nodes marked as word ends; or a set of words + a sorted scan.
Put the words in a set; a word is buildable if every prefix word[:i] is in the set.
Approach: Check prefixes (set or trie).
mistakes: Not checking every prefix of the word, only the longest one.
Breaking ties by length only.
exercises.followup: Return all such words, longest first.

exercises.title: Build a Trie
exercises.prompt:
Implement a prefix tree for lowercase words. Each node has a dict of children and an end-of-word flag.

Requirements:
- `insert(word)`
- `search(word)` → True only for whole inserted words
- `starts_with(prefix)` → True if any word has this prefix
- `words_with_prefix(prefix)` → all inserted words with this prefix, sorted (autocomplete)
hints: insert: walk character by character, creating missing children; mark the last node as end.
search and starts_with both walk the prefix; search also requires node.end.
Approach: One node per character; shared prefixes share nodes.
exercises.cx: O(L) per insert/search for a word of length L

exercises.title: Word Search II
exercises.prompt: Return all words from the list that can be traced on the letter grid by moving up/down/left/right, using each cell at most once per word. Return them sorted.
hints: Searching each word separately repeats a lot of work.
Put all words in a trie; one DFS from each cell follows the trie and stops as soon as no word continues.
Approach: Grid backtracking guided by a trie.
exercises.cx: Exponential in word length, pruned by the trie
mistakes: Running a separate word search for every word (too slow).
Not marking found words, so they are reported twice.
exercises.followup: Prune trie branches once all their words are found.

exercises.title: Concatenated Words
exercises.prompt: Return, in alphabetical order, every word in the list that can be written as a concatenation of at least two shorter words from the same list (words may repeat).
hints: This is Word Break, run for every word, where the dictionary is the list itself (but a word may not use only itself).
Walk the trie from each start position to find every word that begins there; memoize per start position.
Approach: Trie of all words + memoized word-break that counts pieces, keeping words with at least two pieces.
exercises.cx: O(n · L²) time where L is the maximum word length
mistakes: Counting a word as "concatenated" because it matches itself (one piece).
No memoization: exponential on words like "aaaa…".
Trying all pairs of words (misses three-word concatenations and is O(n²)).
exercises.followup: Return, for each concatenated word, one way to split it.

tests.call: len(concatenated_words(["a" * i for i in range(1, 31)]))

exercises.title: Prefixes count as words
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test tr-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
It never checks the end marker, so any prefix of a stored word is “found”
Return "$" in node.

exercises.title: Inserting erases words
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test tr-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
node[ch] = {} REPLACES an existing child, deleting every word below it
Insert "cat" then "car": the second insert wipes out the "a" subtree that held "cat". Use setdefault.

exercises.title: Build an Adjacency List
exercises.prompt: Given n nodes (0..n − 1) and undirected edges, return a dict mapping each node to a sorted list of neighbours.
hints: Start every node with an empty list, including isolated ones.
Start with an empty list for every node; for each edge (u, v) append v to u and u to v, then sort.
Approach: Dict of lists, both directions.
mistakes: Adding each edge in only one direction.
Leaving out nodes with no edges.
exercises.followup: Build an adjacency matrix too and compare memory use.

exercises.title: BFS Order
exercises.prompt: Return the BFS visiting order from `start`. `adj` is a dict of neighbour lists; visit neighbours in the given order.
hints: A deque, a seen set, and mark nodes when you enqueue them.
Use a deque and a visited set; mark a node visited as soon as you add it to the queue.
Approach: Standard BFS.
mistakes: Marking nodes as visited when they are popped instead of when they are queued (duplicates).
Using list.pop(0).
exercises.followup: Return the distance of every node from start.

exercises.title: DFS Order
exercises.prompt: Return the recursive DFS (preorder) visiting order from `start`, visiting neighbours in the given order.
hints: Recursion plus a seen set.
Mark the node visited, record it, then recurse into each unvisited neighbour in order.
Approach: Recursive DFS.
mistakes: Forgetting the visited set, which loops forever on cycles.
Using a stack and getting a different neighbour order than the recursive version.
exercises.followup: Write it with an explicit stack and the same visiting order.

exercises.title: Find if a Path Exists
exercises.prompt: Undirected graph with n nodes and an edge list. Return True if `source` can reach `dest`.
hints: Build an adjacency list, then BFS or DFS from source.
BFS or DFS from source; return True as soon as you reach dest.
Approach: Graph search.
mistakes: Recursion deeper than Python’s limit on long chains (use a stack or BFS).
Treating edges as one-way.
exercises.followup: Answer many (source, dest) queries quickly with union-find.

exercises.title: Flood Fill
exercises.prompt: Starting at (sr, sc), recolor the connected region of the same color (4-directional) to `color`. Return the image.
hints: DFS from the start cell, recoloring cells of the original color.
If the new color equals the old one, return immediately (or you loop forever).
Approach: DFS/BFS over same-colored cells.
mistakes: Recursing forever when the new color equals the old one.
Filling diagonally.
exercises.followup: Return the size of the filled region too.

exercises.title: Find the Town Judge
exercises.prompt: People 1..n; `trust[i] = [a, b]` means a trusts b. The judge trusts nobody and is trusted by everyone else. Return the judge, or -1.
hints: This is about in-degrees and out-degrees of a directed graph.
Count for each person how many trust them and how many they trust.
Approach: Degree counting.
mistakes: Only checking that someone is trusted by everyone (they must also trust nobody).
Treating people as 0-based.
exercises.followup: Solve it with one array of trust scores (in-degree − out-degree).

exercises.title: Keys and Rooms
exercises.prompt: Room 0 is open; `rooms[i]` lists the keys found in room i. Can you visit every room?
hints: Rooms are nodes, keys are directed edges. Is everything reachable from 0?
DFS or BFS from room 0 using the keys as edges; compare the visited count with n.
Approach: Reachability with DFS.
mistakes: Visiting rooms only in index order.
Not marking rooms as visited (loops on keys to visited rooms).
exercises.followup: Return the minimum number of rooms you must enter to collect all keys.

exercises.title: Number of Connected Components
exercises.prompt: Return the number of connected components of an undirected graph with n nodes.
hints: Start a search from every node not yet seen; each start is a new component.
On a long chain, recursive DFS can hit Python’s recursion limit: use an explicit stack or BFS.
Approach: Search from each unvisited node.
mistakes: Forgetting isolated nodes (they are components too).
Starting a search only from node 0.
exercises.followup: Return the size of each component.
